**Identify Indices:** For a sampled point $x$, identify the indices $I_{G_l}$ of the eight voxel corners surrounding $x$ at each grid level $l \in [1, L]$.
**Index Transformation:** Transform the indices from lower-level grids to the corresponding indices in the highest-resolution grid of their group.
This ensures that grid points at identical spatial positions map to the same hash entry despite having different raw indices in different resolutions.
**Feature Retrieval and Interpolation:** Retrieve the $F$-dimensional feature vectors from the hash table entries.
Trilinearly interpolate these vectors to produce a feature vector $f_l$ for each level $l$.
**Concatenation:** Concatenate the $L$ feature vectors into a single vector $y = [f_1; \dots; f_L]$.
*   **Index Mismatch:** Without index transformation, grid points at identical spatial positions in different grids have distinct indices (e.g., $(2,2)$ in $G_{L-1}$ vs $(4,4)$ in $G_L$).
*   **Hash Collisions:** As with all hash-based encodings, collisions may occur.
*   **Memory Efficiency:** MF-NeRF achieves comparable or better reconstruction quality with significantly fewer features than Instant-NGP.
*   **Training Time:** MF-NeRF generally exhibits faster training times due to reduced memory footprint and feature size.
A smaller $N$ (more sharing) reduces memory but may limit the ability to learn distinct features per resolution level.
